item.title: SCP-5923:
item.content:encoded:
There's a lot of things that can be said here, but I think it may suffice to point out first and foremost that a Big Rip scenario is not anomalous. It's a natural consequence of the dark energy equation-of-state parameter being more negative that -1, something that comes out fairly naturally from FLRW equations.

Current best data from the Pantheon sample strongly indicates that w = -1.026, which is within error (not shown here) of w = -1. So while it's unlikely that the big rip will occur, there's nothing in our current understanding of cosmology that precludes this.

There seems to be some reference to "the more people think that the big rip will happen the more negative w becomes", but it's buried in a confusing mess of other thoughts and random diatribes about unrelated things. The fact of the matter is that the cat's sort of out of the bag here, and largely has been since Riess and Perlmutter's discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe in 1998. It's many people's jobs to discuss the value of w - there's been a Nobel prize assigned for that, and it's fairly critical to an ongoing field of physics.

70% of this is describing non-anomalous science. The other 30% is a tangle of self referential procedures and comments designed to scaffold the fundamentally non-anomalous nature of this article.

-1

item.title: SCP-5923: re: your scp
item.content:encoded:
I like the underlying concept. At first I was going to take you to task for just memeing up a novel scientific concept and trying to pass it as an SCP but there is something more here. In total, however, this article suffers from too much speculation and a long trip to arrive at a somewhat subtle pay-day.

I could definitely see this working with a few more refinements. For example, the conprocs are very long and the bit about the meticulous cover-up with amnestics in chocolate and their water is…way off tone for the rest of the piece.

item.title: The Analog Kid:
item.content:encoded:
I'm curious if the interstitial feeling of it now is because it essentially starts in media res, dropping straight into the middle of a massive setting that was only implied at the time but is now well-established, or if it has more to do with the way the crosslinking is perceived

Definitely the former. The crosslinking I can at least accept as something that either was added after the story was completed, or as something that includes parallel storylines that help flesh out the settings.

It's probably not helped by the fact that I am reading this as I make my way through the Asimov’s Lawbringers cycle (mini-canon? series?).

However, just knowing that it's Three Portlands AND Maxwellism AND anart AND Anderson, it's difficult to conceptualize the characters of Myra Rider and Alexis Norwood not having a continuation of this that concludes an epic five part trilogy. Which, as you point out, is literally not a thing that could happen, as this was the starting point for a lot of these settings/characters. But if there's one thing that people love doing, it is backfilling lore for existing characters.

Again, it's more a complaint about the meta aspects of the setting than anything to do with the story, but I feel like the better-defined a setting becomes, the less room people have to fiddle with it. The more fleshed out a setting is, the more the audience (or at least I) implicitly expects for a story in the setting to have some broader impact upon the setting, rather than being just a standalone thing that can exist on its lonesome. Which is a bit of a shame, in my opinion.

To put it another way, the tradition of all written settings weighs like a nightmare on the brains of the living.

item.title: SCP-5762: Re: What makes it an SCP
item.content:encoded: Fair - i wanted to go for a more understated anomalous effect. A lot of Anderson Robotics articles have items that aren't explicitly magical so much as they are tech anomalies. So like, a fully sapient AI that doesn't seem possible with the technology of now seems like it would count as anomalous, since its practically impossible.

item.title: SCP-5923: Second SCP
item.content:encoded:
This is the second article I wrote after The 13 Correlation, which I'll admit suffers from some first-article frays. This has memetic infiltration, pro career cover-ups, cosmic invasion/apocalypse catalyst, auto-creation of reality through observer effects, a play by play of a rapid Big Rip in the Foundation-verse, how it'd interact with various physical anomalies, a precision redaction about one of my favorite early SCPs that seems creepy in a mystical way.

And to top it off, a spook. I didn't expect to find a face in a quasar.

I think I'm hitting a lot of SCP-genre keynotes here while also bringing some fresh spin. I hope you agree.

item.title: SCP-3178:
item.content:encoded:
Here are a few suggestions:

  • "SCP-3178 is seasoning which consists of the composition normally found in factory-made monosodium glutamate with the addition of an unidentified substance." -> "SCP-3178 is a seasoning consisting of factory-made monosodium glutamate and an unidentified substance." It's a minor prose nitpick, but excessive prepositional phrases hurt your clarity and conciseness. I have the same problem, and recommend running your writing through Slickwrite.com to catch it.
  • "the balanced flavour of SCP-3178" is a bit too subjective for my liking. Also, the author can't really know that unless they also tasted it. Maybe say that subjects report the flavor as balanced.
  • "SCP-3178 consumers lose the part of the brain" feels weird. Does that part just cease to exist? It might make more sense to say that it deteriorates
  • SCP-3178-1 feel really disconnected from the rest of the SCP. I'd either remove them or find a way to more smoothly incorporate them.
  • Test logs are good, but a couple of them seem a bit repetitive, maybe remove a couple

On the whole, I think the concept definitely has potential, but there are too many issues for me to give it a +1, so I'm going to make it a non-vote.

item.title: SCP-5762: Re: What makes it an SCP
item.content:encoded:
It's a sapient AI that fits in a surgical robot and is good at what it does.

It's also specifically one from Anderson Robotics, a GOI which makes up for the limitations of modern hardware with literal magic.

item.title: SCP-5134: -1 or 0?
item.content:encoded:
I have written my first comment prior to this one, but the article had since then been revised so yeah.
Anyway, I think this will be my first novote of the site. I understand the SCP, the gist of it is basically the superstition of the number 13 affecting the real world. I like informative SCPs and this one belongs in that category, but since this is an SCP of a superstition, I feel that this SCP could have been more well executed. I'd love to discuss these themes and how, but my verdict for this article is a novote.

item.title: SCP-5134: Hello World
item.content:encoded:
The classic first SCP downvote guantlet. Hope this makes it. Please excuse any perceived impudence for not pipelining work from a new account through the greenlighting and draft review, I have 11 finished articles produced in the last week and figured it'd be better to let things face Darwinian pressure.

The hypermodern themes of informatic SCPs embedded in the corners of our digital reality is something I'm generally interested in so even if this *didn't* land with you, I'm very interested in discussing those themes.

item.title: SCP-5080:
item.content:encoded:
There are parts of this I really like and parts I really don't. By volume most of this is vaguely threatening and mysterious nonsense that mostly seems to be designed to fill space rather than be meaningful.

Which is a shame because I really like the base idea and its implications - Temporal Anomalies fuckery, and the kill-on-sight notice. It's just that most of the flavour put in to support it feels blandly random and actively detracts from the parts I like.

Bold to include graphs and put no colour scales or legends though.
